verdicts.dateTest: Claim: AIIB (actor) approved (did) India financing of US$1.95bn, 1.95bn and 1.87bn (thing) in 2020, 2021 and 2022, against US$0.82bn in 2019 (when). I downloaded the AIIB data file on 2026-09-26 (HTTP 200, 213 KB) and grouped Approved India rows by the 'date' field. The result matches the record exactly: 2017 1,074; 2018 1,145; 2019 820; 2020 1,950; 2021 1,946; 2022 1,869; 2023 1,105; 2024 1,058; 2025 1,640 (US$m). Sovereign 2020–22 = 1,750 + 1,896 + 1,719 = US$5,365m, which matches the 'd' field's US$5.36bn. The window is right: Galwan was June 2020, and the CARES approval (2020-06-16) and all other rows fall inside 2020–22. One caveat: grouping by URL-path year gives different yearly totals (2020 = 2,398; 2022 = 1,421). Two India projects, Assam Secondary Roads and HORC, have 2020 paths but 2022 approval dates. On the Assam page, concept review is 2020-12-11 and financing approval is 2022-06-29. An 18-month cycle is normal and is not evidence of a stall.
verdicts.identityTest: Every row is economy = 'India' in AIIB's own file, so the lender (fin:aiib) is correct. The target node is wrong for the full amount. The US$5.77bn ('≈US$5.8bn') includes US$400m of nonsovereign approvals that went to private borrowers, not to the Union or the states: HDFC line of credit US$200m (2020), Enel Green solar US$50m (2021), Kotak Infrastructure Investment Fund US$100m (2022) and Solar IPP equity US$50m (2022). Only the sovereign US$5.365bn can be attributed to min:ministry-of-finance and the states.
verdicts.baseRate: This is not a discriminating property. AIIB's total approvals across the bank more than doubled: US$4.08bn (2019) → 9.30bn (2020) → 9.30bn (2021) → 6.62bn (2022). India's rise, 2.38x from 2019 to 2020, matches the bank-wide 2.28x. The better test is India's share, and it did not fall: 20.1% (2019), 21.0% (2020), 20.9% (2021), 28.3% (2022). That supports the 'no slowdown' reading more strongly than raw totals do. The share then fell to 9.8% in 2023 and 13.1% in 2024, while bank-wide approvals rose to US$11.2bn. Symmetry control from the SPEC (BJP-run vs opposition-run states): the 2020–22 state-level approvals are mixed. Assam, Gujarat and Haryana (BJP) got US$1.39bn; Kerala, West Bengal, Punjab and Tamil Nadu (opposition or regional parties) got about US$0.98bn. There is no party skew in either direction.
verdicts.denialFound: No accusation is being made, so there is nothing to deny. The response on record is from an Indian official quoted by Mint in July 2020 and reproduced in The Diplomat (2021-06-14): "We are not taking money from China but from the multilateral development bank. I don't see any structural change in our engagement with AIIB because of our tensions with China." https://thediplomat.com/2021/06/amid-tensions-with-china-india-proceeding-with-aiib-funded-projects/ . The record also cites SCMP (2021-06-04): AIIB president Jin Liqun said loans to India were maintained. I did not re-open the SCMP article.
verdicts.innocentReading: The pandemic facility was open to every AIIB member, and approvals bank-wide doubled in 2020–21. India's share stayed near 20–28%, so India's totals simply tracked the bank. The record's version of this reading has two errors. First, India's COVID Crisis Recovery Facility (CRF) loans were US$2.25bn in four loans, not US$1.75bn in three: CARES US$750m (2020), Health Systems US$500m (2020), Social Protection US$500m (2021), and Vaccines US$500m (2022, tagged 'CRF-Public Health'). So 2022 is inflated by the facility as well. Second, excluding CRF, the series is 820 → 700 → 1,446 → 1,369 → 1,105 → 1,058. Non-COVID approvals in 2020 were slightly below 2019. The 2023–24 dip happened while bank-wide approvals rose, so it is India-specific in relative terms. 'India's pivot to ADB/World Bank policy loans' is not sourced anywhere in the record.
verdicts.reason: The core analytic claim survives. AIIB's own primary data file reproduces every yearly figure, and India's share of AIIB approvals held or rose in 2020–22. That makes 'no post-Galwan slowdown in approvals' a sound analytic reading. The Diplomat independently found that "I did not come across evidence of any project being halted due to government intervention." Analytic is the right tier: the numbers are documented, but the 'no slowdown' conclusion is an inference, and approval data cannot show pipeline attrition. I could not refute the claim, but its benefit clause and innocent reading have factual errors that must be fixed. The ≈US$5.8bn credited to 'the Union and states' includes US$400m of private nonsovereign deals. 'Drew' overstates what the data shows, since approvals are not disbursements. 'Bilateral ties curtailed' goes beyond the cited source, which says only 'a few' Chinese investments were halted and that 'New Delhi has done little' on imports. The CRF amount is understated.
verdicts.corrections: 1) benefit.how: change 'drew ≈US$5.8bn of AIIB approvals' to 'had ≈US$5.37bn of sovereign AIIB approvals in 2020–22 (US$5.77bn including US$0.4bn nonsovereign to HDFC, Enel, Kotak fund and a solar IPP)'. 'Drew' should become 'were approved for'. 2) benefit.amountCr: 42949 is based on 5,765; recompute on sovereign 5,365 at the same rate (~₹74.5/US$), giving ≈39,970. 3) innocentReading: change 'US$1.75bn in three loans' to 'US$2.25bn in four loans (2020 CARES 750, 2020 Health 500, 2021 Social Protection 500, 2022 Vaccines 500)'; change '2020–21 totals inflated' to '2020–22 totals inflated'. Either remove 'India's pivot to larger ADB/World Bank policy loans' or source it. Note that non-CRF approvals in 2020 (US$700m) were below 2019 (US$820m). 4) d: add India's share of AIIB approvals (20.1 / 21.0 / 20.9 / 28.3% for 2019–22; 9.8 / 13.1% for 2023–24) against bank-wide totals (4.08 / 9.30 / 9.30 / 6.62 / 11.25 / 8.09 US$bn). The share is the non-trivial comparison, and it shows the 2023–24 dip is India-specific because bank-wide lending rose. 5) Change the phrase 'bilateral economic ties with China were curtailed' to 'some Chinese investment was restricted or halted (The Diplomat: "only a few")', or add a primary source such as Press Note 3 (2020). 6) Add the Mint/Diplomat official quote as the response field. 7) Note in d that year grouping uses the file's 'date' field, not the URL path year (HORC and Assam roads carry 2020 paths but were approved in 2022).

verdicts.dateTest: Claim restated: "ADB's top-three recipient states in 2016–21 were run by BJP, INC and JD(U)", and "AIIB's sovereign approvals for India in 2017–26 went to states run by BJP, INC, DMK, LDF, TMC, AAP and TDP/YSRCP". The ADB side mostly holds. MP: BJP Jan 2016–Dec 2018, INC Dec 2018–23 Mar 2020, BJP after that, so about 4.7 of 6 years BJP. Rajasthan: BJP (Raje) until 17 Dec 2018, INC (Gehlot) after that, so about 2.96 years BJP against 3.04 years INC. "INC-led for most of the window" is true by only about 1% and is really an even split. Bihar: JD(U)-led for the whole window, but the record's `d` field is wrong. It says "JD(U)-BJP except Aug 2022–Jan 2024" and leaves out the JD(U)-RJD-INC Mahagathbandhan government of Nov 2015–Jul 2017. The AIIB side fails the date test on three party labels, checked against approval dates on the AIIB project pages. (1) Punjab Municipal Services was approved 27 Apr 2021, when INC (Amarinder Singh) ran Punjab. AAP took over in Mar 2022, and no AIIB approval for Punjab comes after that, so "AAP" is wrong. (2) The Andhra Pradesh approvals (24x7 Power 2017, Urban Water 2018, Rural Roads 2018) all fall under TDP. YSRCP (May 2019–Jun 2024) has no AIIB approval, so "YSRCP" is wrong. (3) Maharashtra MUTP-III was approved 26 Sep 2019 under the BJP-Shiv Sena government (Fadnavis). The MVA government (Nov 2019–Jun 2022) has no AIIB approval, and the later approvals (MUTP-3A 2023, Metro Line 5 2024, MAHA RE 2025) fall under Shinde-BJP or Fadnavis, so "MVA" is wrong. DMK (Chennai approvals of 23 Sep 2021, 11 Nov 2021 and 2023), LDF (Kerala 2021 and 2024) and TMC (West Bengal 2019 and 2022) are correct. The claim leaves out INC-run Karnataka (Bangalore Metro R6, 2017) and does not name Haryana (BJP), MP (BJP, approved 11 Apr 2018) or Manipur (BJP, 2024).
verdicts.identityTest: The entities match the sources. The CPSFR (ADB IED-style final review, April 2022, para 222) names "Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, and Bihar" as top-three states. The AIIB data file lists India sovereign projects with state names in their titles, and I count 12 named states (AP, Gujarat, Maharashtra, TN, Kerala, WB, Assam, Punjab, Karnataka, MP, Haryana, Manipur), which fits "~12". The party labels are the analyst's own addition and appear in neither source. The actor who approves is the lender's board, and the borrower of record is the Union of India (DEA). The state government is the executing or implementing agency, not the counterparty. The record should say this so that "state run by party X" is not read as "party X borrowed".
verdicts.baseRate: The BJP or NDA held CM posts in a majority of states for most of 2017–26 (roughly 12–21 of ~30), so any spread of state-level lending would show "BJP states" heavily, and that fact does not discriminate. I summed AIIB sovereign approvals with a state in the title by the CM's party on the approval date. NDA-run states got about US$4.2bn: Assam 1,151, Maharashtra 1,885, Gujarat 579, Manipur 352, MP 140, Haryana 128. Opposition-run states got about US$3.5bn: TN-DMK 1,323 plus AIADMK 100, AP-TDP 1,015, Kerala-LDF 352, Karnataka-INC 335, WB-TMC 280, Punjab-INC 105. That is about 55:45 and roughly in line with the number of states each side ran. For ADB, two of the three top states (MP and Rajasthan) were both INC-run from Dec 2018 to Mar 2020, which is when the low-income share was at its peak (70% in 2019). The fleet control (UPA vs NDA; BJP vs opposition states) gives no partisan picture either way. Per-capita and prior-lending normalisation has not been done, which the record already flags as a gap.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable: this is a null analytic finding and nobody is accused. No party was asked. No statement from ADB, AIIB or DEA on partisan allocation was searched for or found.
verdicts.innocentReading: ADB's own CPS 2013–2017 set a target of 40–50% of lending for lower-income states, and ADB had worked in MP and Bihar since 2003 and in Rajasthan since CPS 2009–12. So income category and long-standing state relationships, not the ruling party, explain why low-income states dominate. Both lenders' sovereign loans go through DEA, which ranks state proposals largely on project readiness. Two cautions on the record's wording. First, the source's word is "added that ... would be 40-50%", which is a strategy target and not a "mandate" or "rule". Second, the target explains why low-income states dominate but not why these particular three rank at the top, so "mechanically produces MP/Rajasthan/Bihar" overstates the case.
verdicts.reason: The claim survives in its conclusion but not in its wording. I checked the ADB source verbatim. CPSFR para 222 says: "The CPS 2013-2017 added that overall ADB lending to the lower income states would be 40-50% of the total ADB lending to India during the CPS period ... Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, and Bihar have been the top-three states that received highest share of the ADB program in 2016-2021." I opened the AIIB data file and six approval pages. Once each approval is dated, three of the eight party labels in the AIIB list fail the date test: AAP, YSRCP and MVA had no AIIB approval while in office. Karnataka-INC is missing from the list. After correction, the approval split is still about 55:45 between NDA-run and opposition-run states, and the ADB top-three include two states that were INC-run in the peak year. So the null finding ("no partisan skew visible, unnormalised") still stands. The claim should be published only with the label corrections. Tier stays analytic: it is our own comparison, it has an innocentReading, it implies no wrongdoing, and it has not been normalised.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim: ADB/AIIB financed ReNew in 2014, 2016, 2017, 2025 and 2025. All five dates check out against the sources. 47926-014 PDS: "Approval 16 May 2014", borrower "ReNew Private Limited". 50195-001 PDS: "Approval 02 Dec 2016". 51210-001 PDS: "Approval 12 Dec 2017". ADB release: "(10 November 2025) — ADB has signed a $331 million finance package with ReNew Vyoman Power Private Limited". AIIB 000967: "FINANCING APPROVAL November 7, 2025 … FINANCING APPROVED FUNDING USD100 million". The "inherited" label for the Ostro Kutch loan fails the date test, though. The PDS says "The Project was acquired by Renew Power Private Limited in March 2018". ADB's own IATI India file (https://www.adb.org/iati/iati-activities-in.xml, LN3622) records the US$100m commitment on 2018-09-25, six months after ReNew took control. ADB approved the loan while Ostro was independent but committed it to a ReNew-owned SPV, so it is not a loan ReNew merely inherited. The claim also leaves out one engagement inside the window. ADB 54165-001, the "ReNew Power COVID-19 Liquidity Support Project", has borrower "ReNew Private Limited", a debt security of "INR 3,738.00 million" and "Approval 29 Jul 2020" (PDS https://www.adb.org/projects/54165-001/main; IATI LN7639).
verdicts.identityTest: The entities hold up. ReNew Private Limited (formerly ReNew Power Pvt Ltd / ReNew Power Ventures) is the borrower on 47926-014 and 54165-001 and the sponsor on 50195-001, 51210-001 and AIIB 000967. The borrowing SPVs are ReNew Vyoman Power Pvt Ltd for ADB and "ReNew Vyoman Private Limited" for AIIB. They are the same project, and AIIB says it is "co-financed with ADB". One correction: on 51210-001 the Borrower/Company is still Ostro Kutch Wind Private Limited, and ReNew Private Limited appears as Project Sponsor, not as "Company". The energy:renew evidence line and c032 "d" both get this wrong. On Adani, ADB's IATI India file (405 activities) has no Adani entity, and AIIB's all-projects-data.js lists no Adani borrower among its India nonsovereign entries. "AGPCGPL" is AG&P City Gas, a name collision the file already notes. The absence is confirmed.
verdicts.baseRate: Denominator: the Indian private counterparties in ADB's IATI India file plus AIIB's India nonsovereign list. Repeat counterparties are common in financial intermediaries. IIFL Home Finance appears 3 times (ADB 2021, ADB 2025, AIIB 2025). Shriram appears at least 3 times (ADB 2022 and 2024, AIIB "Facility II" 2026). Cholamandalam (2018, 2025), Aavas (2020, 2025), Krsnaa (2021, 2025) and Suguna (2019, 2020) appear twice each. Counted as a group, Tata is comparable to ReNew: ADB Tata Power wind 2007, Mundra/CGPL 2008, Tata Capital Growth Fund II 2019, TPDDL 2023 and Tata Energy Access Solar 2025, plus AIIB Tata Cleantech 2019, for about 6 engagements. At single-company level ReNew is the top repeat counterparty, with 6 ADB engagements (2014, 2016, 2017/18, 2020, 2025 ADB, 2025 AIIB). So "most repeated" survives and is slightly understated. But the symmetric control (the Tata group) produces a similar picture, and roughly 10–15% of private counterparties are repeat borrowers. The property picks out ReNew but says nothing about wrongdoing, which is consistent with the analytic tier.
verdicts.denialFound: No denial exists, and none is needed: the claim is analytic and alleges no wrongdoing. Neither ADB nor ReNew was asked. The closest on-record statement is ADB VP Bhargav Dasgupta in the 2025-11-10 release: "This landmark project reflects ADB's long-standing partnership with ReNew, which has spanned multiple investments and initiatives over the years." Sumant Sinha: "Our long-standing collaboration with ADB has enabled us to continually push the boundaries…" (https://www.adb.org/news/adb-renew-sign-331-million-deal-solar-wind-bess-power-plant-generating-24-7-clean-energy-india). Both parties acknowledge the repeat relationship openly.
verdicts.innocentReading: ReNew is India's second-largest IPP ("second largest Independent Power Producer (IPP) in India, with a total portfolio of 18.2 GW" — AIIB 000967). MDB private windows concentrate on a few large, investment-grade sponsors with a known corporate ESMS. ADB's CPS explicitly aimed to scale up nonsovereign renewables. The Kutch project came out of India's first competitive wind auction (the PDS says so), and the 2025 plant sells under a 25-year SECI PPA at a fixed ₹4.69/kWh. The 2014 equity was exited in 2016 "with satisfactory returns" (CPSFR). The same pattern repeats for Tata and the NBFC borrowers. The claim's innocent-reading text goes further than the evidence in two places. First, it says pricing was "market-based OCR" as though that were sourced, but loan pricing is not on the project pages, so this is ADB's stated policy for nonsovereign lending, not a checked term. Second, "on competitively auctioned SECI PPAs" covers only Kutch and Vyoman. The 2014 equity and the 2020 working-capital debenture were corporate-level and had no PPA, and the 2016 SPVs had mixed offtakers.
verdicts.reason: The main finding survives and gets stronger: ReNew is the most repeated single Indian private counterparty of ADB and AIIB, and Adani Green has no ADB or AIIB record, which the IATI file and AIIB data confirm. The claim as written still fails on facts it can be checked against. (1) The "≈₹4,400 crore cumulative" figure matches neither the file's own components (295+669+642+2,932+886 = ₹5,424 crore, which is the benefit.amountCr in the same record) nor the corrected total. The corrected total is about ₹5,950 crore: 295 + 818 (the 50195 PDS closed/committed amounts including LEAP 8324 US$22.16m, which c031 omits: 10+29.10+22.13+12.18+25.14+22.16 = US$120.7m) + 642 + 374 (the omitted 2020 INR 3,738m COVID debenture) + 2,932 + 886. (2) The list leaves out ADB 54165-001 (2020), so there are 6 engagements (ADB 5 + AIIB 1), not 5. (3) "Inherited Ostro Kutch loan" is misleading, because ADB committed the loan on 2018-09-25, after ReNew acquired Ostro in March 2018. (4) The two 2025 items are one co-financed project, not two independent choices. With these corrections the claim stays analytic. It becomes neither kill nor documented, because "most repeated" is our own inference over the lenders' records.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim restated: the Union government (DEA, Ministry of Finance; Modi PM since 2014, Sitharaman FM since 2019) borrowed US$1.25bn from AIIB in May–June 2020. Tenure overlaps, so the date test passes. The two loans need separate dates. (1) Health loan, US$500m: the AIIB page gives "APPROVAL DATE" May 7, 2020. The only source for signing is FPJ: "the agreement was signed on May 8, 2020". That is five weeks before the 15 June Galwan clash, though after the standoff began in early May. It fits "amid the standoff" but not "while soldiers were killed". (2) CARES, US$750m: the AIIB page gives approval June 16, 2020, one day after the clash. The only source for signing is FPJ: "the loan agreement was signed on June 19 when the country was mourning the loss of its soldiers." So only one of the two loans falls after Galwan. Its timing was set by the ADB-led programme it co-finances, which ADB approved and signed on 28 Apr 2020 (ADB PDS). FPJ also says "the second loan discussion started in May 2020". Both points predate the clash.
verdicts.identityTest: Pass. The actor is the Government of India through the Department of Economic Affairs, which both the AIIB CARES page and the ADB PDS 54182-001 name as executing agency. The lender is AIIB, a multilateral bank headquartered in Beijing, not the PRC state. The narrative's wording "ADB lead cofinancier" is correct only for CARES. The health loan (AIIB, US$500m) was co-financed with the World Bank. The AIIB page says: "AIIB (the Bank) will co-finance this project with the World Bank (WB)".
verdicts.baseRate: Borrowing from AIIB was not unusual for India. FPJ says India "continues to be the largest borrower of AIIB... around USD 3.6 billion which is around 25 per cent of the AIIB's overall lending". India had been borrowing sovereign money from AIIB since 2017, and the COVID Crisis Recovery Facility was open to all members. Within India's own AIIB history, then, a 2020 loan is close to 100%: non-discriminating. The UPA control does not apply because AIIB began operating in 2016. The symmetric control does apply. The same "controlled by the largest shareholder" lens would call the same-month World Bank co-financed health loan and the ADB CARES loans "US-controlled" or "Japan-controlled". That would make the characterisation a statement about multilateral banks in general, not about this government.
verdicts.denialFound: Government: an anonymous Indian official quoted by Mint, cited in The Diplomat of 2021-06-14 (https://thediplomat.com/2021/06/amid-tensions-with-china-india-proceeding-with-aiib-funded-projects/): "We are not taking money from China but from the multilateral development bank. I don't see any structural change in our engagement with AIIB because of our tensions with China." The Mint original was not opened. Lender: Jin Liqun, via SCMP 2021-06-04 (https://www.scmp.com/economy/global-economy/article/3136109/china-backed-aiib-maintained-loans-india-during-border). He said AIIB "kept lending to India despite domestic pressure", and SCMP reports him "refuting claims the lender is simply a tool for China's strategic interests". No on-record ministerial answer to the Galwan-timing charge was opened. The record does not name who made the "China-controlled" charge, so nobody can be shown to have been asked.
verdicts.innocentReading: Both AIIB loans were add-ons to programmes led by other banks. The health loan co-financed a World Bank project, approved 7 May. CARES co-financed ADB's US$1.5bn CARES programme, which ADB signed on 28 Apr 2020. Their approval dates followed AIIB's COVID-facility processing cycle, which began in April–May, before the clash. The money came from a multilateral bank in which India is the second-largest shareholder (7.6% per FPJ) and India's largest source of AIIB lending. It paid for health response and PMGKY cash transfers. Signing three days after Galwan reflects a timetable already under way, not a decision taken after the clash.
verdicts.reason: The narrative survives as a two-sided "contested" record. The borrowing is on primary record: the AIIB pages show US$500m approved 2020-05-07 and US$750m approved 2020-06-16, and ADB PDS 54182-001 lists "Co-financer AIIB: US$ 750 million". The claimant's side and the counter-side are both put fairly. The source chain has one load-bearing fault. The headline figure "₹9,200 crore" appears in none of the four cited sources. FPJ, the only outlet the record credits with the rupee figures, gives only dollars: "USD 1,250 million". The ₹9,200 cr is an internal sum of c003 (₹5,521 cr) and c004 (₹3,676 cr). Both of those are mislabelled "as stated by FPJ" when they are our own conversions. The signing dates (05-08 and 06-19) rest on FPJ alone, and FPJ contradicts itself on amounts ("USD 500 million and USD 250 million" against a total of 1,250). Those dates are therefore reported, not documented. Finally, "contested" is a narrative calibration status, not a tier. Where one tier value is required, this is our own two-sided judgement, i.e. analytic, with the component loan edges documented (approvals) or reported (signings). These faults need correcting, but none of them overturns the narrative's verdict.
verdicts.corrections:
1. Narrative text: replace "₹9,200 crore" with "US$1.25bn (≈₹9,200 crore at ≈₹73.5/US$, our conversion)". Or cite a source that actually states ₹9,200/9,202 crore, such as the originating political claim or a Parliament answer. None of the current sources states it.
2. Change "borrowing documented (... signed 2020-05-08 ...; ... signed 2020-06-19)" to "approvals documented (AIIB: US$500m approved 2020-05-07; US$750m approved 2020-06-16); signing dates 2020-05-08 / 2020-06-19 reported (FPJ only)".

verdicts.dateTest: Written as a claim: "RCom (IBC 2019), Aircel (IBC 2018) and Lanco (CIRP 2017) entered insolvency after borrowing from CDB/China Eximbank in 2008–2015; Sasan kept servicing." The loans come before each insolvency (RCom 2008/2011/2012 → 2019; Aircel 2015-03-27 → 2018; Lanco 2010 → 2017), so the dates pass. Two problems remain. First, the only evidence that Sasan kept servicing is the US Ex-Im OIG report, which records the first US$28.4m payment to US Ex-Im in March 2015. That is a different lender from the Chinese syndicate, and nothing in the record covers Sasan's servicing from 2015 to 2020, even though the edge runs to 2020. Second, the label says Sasan was "refinanced" while the text says it "continued servicing". These contradict each other and neither is sourced for the Chinese tranche.

(#54362, 92020, 92021 = Sasan), Aircel Ltd. (#54342) and Lanco Infratech Ltd. (#53777). Identities are fine. The claim fails on how the set was chosen. It is not "the four largest". (1) Counting only policy banks (CDB + China Eximbank): RCom ≈US$3,296m, Reliance Power/Sasan US$667m, Aircel US$462m, Essar Energy US$300m (#96694, China Eximbank 2013), Sistema Shyam US$255m (#67448), then Lanco US$200m in sixth place. (2) Counting all Chinese banks: RCom US$3,605m, Sasan US$1,000m, Aircel US$462m, APML US$333m (#53783/54345), SSTL US$325m, Essar US$300m, RIL US$220m, Vedanta US$210m, then Lanco US$200m in ninth. Lanco only reaches the top four by adding the US$600m Anpara/Himavat MoU (#53778), which AidData codes "Pipeline: Pledge" and marks not for aggregates. If pledges count, IndiGo (US$2.6bn), SRM Energy (US$1.19bn), IDBI (US$1.2bn) and Essar (US$1bn) all rank above Lanco. The claim text also says "policy banks", but the RCom figure of US$3.6bn and Sasan's "≈US$1bn Chinese share" both include ICBC or BOC, which are commercial banks. verdicts.baseRate: With a set chosen consistently, the "3 of 4" figure does not hold. Top four by policy-bank lending (RCom, Sasan, Aircel, Essar Energy): 2 in IBC (RCom, Aircel), Sasan unverified after 2015, and Essar Energy plc itself never went through Indian IBC. Top four by all Chinese banks (RCom, Sasan, Aircel, APML): 2 of 4. APML (Adani Power Maharashtra, Tiroda) never entered IBC. Every recommended private borrower of US$100m or more (10 entities: RCom, Sasan, Aircel, APML, SSTL, Essar, RIL, Vedanta, Lanco, CLP): 3 in formal insolvency (RCom, Aircel, Lanco), or 4 if you count SSTL, which RCom absorbed in 2016–17 and which went into RCom's 2019 IBC. That is roughly 30–40%, a moderate rate that is worth publishing, not 75%. For context, other lenders to the same borrowers lost money too: SBI-led Indian consortia (RCom, Aircel, Lanco) and SEK/Nordic Investment Bank (co-lenders on Aircel). The losses do not single out Chinese lenders.

verdicts.innocentReading: The record's own innocent reading holds and is stronger than the claim itself. Chinese policy banks lent equipment-tied credit to the most leveraged 2G-era telecom groups and merchant coal-power groups of 2008–2015. Those two sectors collapsed for everyone after the 2012 2G-licence cancellation (Supreme Court, February 2012), the Jio tariff war (2016–17) and the coal-block cancellations and shortages (2014). Indian public-sector banks lost more to the same borrowers. Where Chinese banks lent to regulated or diversified borrowers (Adani Power Maharashtra with a PPA, CLP Jhajjar, RIL, Vedanta, and the SOEs Air India, GAIL, ONGC and SBI), they did not end up in insolvency. So the result reflects which sectors they lent to, not anything about the banks as lenders.
verdicts.reason:
The main error is the denominator. "The four largest Indian private borrowers from Chinese policy banks" is false as stated. In AidData GCDF 3.0 (the claim's own source), Lanco's US$200m ranks sixth among policy-bank borrowers and ninth among borrowers from all Chinese banks. It only enters the top four by counting a non-binding US$600m pledge, and applied consistently that rule would bring in larger pledges such as IndiGo, SRM, IDBI and Essar. With the correct top four (Essar Energy or APML in place of Lanco), 2 of 4 entered insolvency, not 3. A mixed selection rule produced the headline ratio. Other problems:
- None of the four cited sources supports Lanco's 2017 or Aircel's 2018 insolvency. AidData #53777 says only that Lanco's projects were "delayed … financial problems", and #54342 says nothing about Aircel's insolvency.
- The evidence that Sasan kept servicing is a 2015 payment to US Ex-Im, not to the Chinese lenders.
- The label ("refinanced") contradicts the text ("continued servicing").
The underlying facts (RCom, Aircel and Lanco insolvencies) are true public record, so the claim should be restated as an analytic with the correct denominator, not killed.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim: NCRTC opened Package 4 financial bids on 2020-06-12 and issued the LOA to STEC on 2020-12-09. The dates hold. NH/PTI: bids were invited on 2019-11-09. UTN: "the Technical bids for this contract package were opened on 16 March 2020". UTN is dated 2020-06-12 and says "NCRTC has today opened financial bids". ADB Procurement Plan Rev 7.0, Pkg-4: "153,570,000.00 09-Dec-2020 Awarded to M/s Shanghai Tunnel Engineering Co. Ltd. LOA Date: 09-Dec-2020". Galwan was 2020-06-15. PIB Order was 2020-07-23. So "bids pre-dated the clash and the Order" is true of Galwan. It is not true of the LAC standoff as a whole, which began in early May 2020, before the financial-bid opening. The award came after both. PIB confirms the transition rule that matters here: "If this stage has been crossed, ordinarily the tenders will be cancelled and the process started de novo." Package 4 had crossed that stage, so cancellation was the default the Order prescribed. The claim's counterfactual premise is therefore sourced, but only if the Order reached a tender financed by ADB under an existing loan agreement. That point is unverified: the Order's annexures (pibcms.nic.in) could not be retrieved, DNS failed, and the record itself lists this as a gap.

UTN names "Shanghai Tunnel Engineering Co. Ltd. (STEC)" with the same scope, including Anand Vihar. NCRTC is the awarder in all three press sources. The claim says Afcons was L5. ADB PP confirms Afcons won Pkg-8, the Meerut TBM tunnels, at est. US$208.38m, LOA 2020-11-26. CONFLICT: Tribune (Dikshit) says "The Chinese company's quote was a few crores less than that of the Turkish company Gulermak", which makes Gülermak the runner-up. UTN has L&T as L2 at ₹1,170 cr and Gülermak as L3 at ₹1,326 cr. NH/PTI does not name L&T or give its price. The "L&T lost by ₹44 cr" leg therefore rests on UTN alone, and a cited source contradicts it. It is not "reported ×2" as the STEC node claims.
verdicts.baseRate: It is not discriminating that the L1 bidder won. Under ADB open competitive bidding with international advertisement, the award goes to the lowest-evaluated responsive bidder essentially 100% of the time. A Chinese firm winning a lender-financed Indian contract is not new either: the record's own WB notices list Baoding Tianwei (2011), Xian XD and Sichuan Yibin (2012), TBEA Shenyang (2012) under UPA, and Beijing NRRDI/CRSC (2016) under NDA. So the property appears under both governments. Of the 19 awarded RRTS packages (ADB PP), STEC won 1, worth US$153.57m or 12.5% of value. L&T won 3 (35.1%) and Afcons 2 (28.9%). The L1 margin of about 3.8–3.9% over L2 is ordinary in competitive tunnelling tenders. Symmetry check against the SPEC control of Chinese finance vs Japanese ODA: JICA-tied WDFC procurement restricts the field to Japanese firms by design. Under the same "who gained" lens that would show a larger, structural benefit to the lender's nationals, so the STEC case is the milder one.
verdicts.denialFound: NCRTC spokesperson via PTI, National Herald, 2021-01-04: "Approvals have to be taken at various levels for bids that are funded by multilateral agencies. This bid was also awarded following the set procedure and guidelines." PTI/NH also: "According to the ADB's procurement guidelines, vendors from all member countries of the bank are eligible to participate in the bidding process without any discrimination." (https://www.nationalheraldindia.com/india/chinese-firm-given-contract-worth-rs-1126-crore-for-delhi-meerut-rail-tunnel-even-as-lac-standoff-continues). Neither the claim nor the record contains a response from STEC, ADB, or DoE/MoF on whether a waiver or exemption from the Order was used. It is not known whether they were asked. No wrongdoing is alleged, so nothing needs denying beyond NCRTC's procedural statement.
verdicts.innocentReading: This was an ADB-financed international competitive bid, and the lender's rules made all member-country firms eligible, China included. Technical bids were opened in March 2020, and the financial bids on 2020-06-12, before Galwan and before the 23 July Order. STEC was L1 by a few percent, and NCRTC waited about six months for multilevel approvals, including ADB's, before issuing the LOA. The loan agreement arguably took precedence over a domestic GFR order issued later. Cancelling would have risked a breach of the lender's procurement rules and delayed an 82-km corridor on which every other civil package had already been awarded. This is a routine procedural outcome, not a favour.
verdicts.reason: The claim's core facts survive. STEC was L1 at ₹1,126 cr (UTN, NH/PTI), and the LOA was issued on 2020-12-09 at est. US$153.57m (ADB PP, primary). PIB's text confirms the "ordinarily cancelled and started de novo" rule. NCRTC's response is on the record. But the claim as written fails on four specific points. (1) The ₹1,126.89 cr figure does not appear in any cited source. UTN and NH both say "Rs 1,126 crore", and ADB gives only a US$ estimate. The .89 figure is also inconsistent with the "₹44 cr" gap: 1,170 − 1,126.89 = 43.11. (2) "≥₹44 cr" is not a floor. A de-novo rebid could have come in lower, and nothing shows L&T would have held ₹1,170 cr. At best it is "≈₹43–44 cr if bids were unchanged". (3) "6–12 months" has no source anywhere in the record. (4) The idea that cancellation was available "under the July 2020 Order" assumes the Order reached a tender financed by ADB under an existing loan agreement. The record's own gap entry admits the annexures that would settle this were not read. One more problem: a cited source (Tribune) names Gülermak, not L&T, as the narrow runner-up, and the claim does not disclose this conflict. The ledger row stays analytic, but only once these numbers are corrected.

On the ~6-month cut: "three-year term ... was to conclude this October." BS 2025-05-03 also has "sources cited in the report [Indian Express] suggest Subramanian had raised concerns about certain IMF datasets" and the Pakistan-vote timing. It is a conjunction of different evidence grades, though. The termination and who decided it are documented: an ACC order, an on-record IMF spokesperson, and wide independent coverage (Indian Express, HT, Mint, TOI). The reasons rest only on unnamed sources, and a named party (Congress) asserts impropriety. Keeping "alleged" for the combined text is correct and conservative. verdicts.dateTest: As written: IMF lent about US$7bn to the Ministry of Finance, secured against 67t of gold (47t Bank of England, 20t UBS), in May 1991. The actor window overlaps: the Chandra Shekhar caretaker government ran until 21 Jun 1991 and the Rao/Manmohan Singh government from 21 Jun 1991. The dates inside the claim are wrong, though. Indian Express (Shaji Vikraman, 5 Apr 2017, which Wikipedia itself cites) says: "Between July 4 and 18, 1991, the RBI pledged 46.91 tonnes of gold with the Bank of England and the Bank of Japan to raise $400 million." That means the 47t tranche was July 1991, not May. Only the roughly 20t SBI-held confiscated gold, handled as a sale-and-repurchase with UBS for about $200m, belongs to May 1991. The IMF drawings were also not in May 1991. From memory, and not verified here because imf.org returns 403: a first-credit-tranche stand-by plus a CCFF drawing were made in January 1991, and the main 20-month stand-by arrangement was approved in October 1991, under the new government.
verdicts.identityTest: The counterparty is wrong. The source for the gold facts says it was pledged to "the Bank of England and the Bank of Japan", central banks that "insisted on physical delivery of gold". It was not pledged to the IMF. The UBS tranche was a sale with a repurchase option, which is not a pledge. Also, the 20t was confiscated gold given to SBI, not RBI reserves. So the gold secured bilateral central-bank and bank financing, not the IMF stand-by or CCFF. The borrower node min:ministry-of-finance is acceptable for IMF drawings (Government of India). The gold transactions were RBI and SBI transactions, not MoF's. Even the Wikipedia page contradicts its own "$7bn from the IMF" line in the same sentence: the gold was airlifted "to raise $600 million".
verdicts.baseRate: Borrowing from the IMF with conditionality during a balance-of-payments crisis was near-universal for 1980s–90s developing-country crisis borrowers, so it does not discriminate. Gold pledged as collateral to central banks is rarer, but it is not an IMF feature: the IMF lends to members against quota and does not take gold collateral. Symmetry: the same crisis borrowing ran across a Janata Dal (S)/Congress-supported caretaker government (January and May 1991) and a Congress government (July and October 1991). No partisan asymmetry is available.
verdicts.denialFound: None found; nobody was asked. Not a wrongdoing claim. Contrary factual reporting exists: the Indian Express (5 Apr 2017, https://indianexpress.com/article/explained/in-fact-how-govts-pledged-gold-to-pull-economy-back-from-the-brink/) places the 46.91t pledge in July 1991 and names BoE and BoJ as the lenders against it. It also says the gold was repurchased before December 1991.
verdicts.innocentReading: This is the ordinary sequence of a balance-of-payments emergency. India drew IMF resources (January 1991 CCFF plus first-tranche stand-by, October 1991 stand-by), which carried standard conditionality. Separately, it raised short-term bridge money by pledging or selling gold to BoE, BoJ and UBS, because commercial markets were closed after the rating downgrades. The two strands happened at the same time but were separate transactions. Merging them ("IMF loan secured by gold") is a popular myth. It inflates the "IMF dictated reforms" story by implying the IMF held India's gold.
verdicts.reason: Fatal: the claim's load-bearing link, that the IMF loan was "secured against ~67 tonnes of pledged gold", is false according to the reporting Wikipedia itself cites. The gold secured about $400m from the Bank of England and Bank of Japan (July 4–18, 1991) and about $200m through an SBI–UBS sale-and-repurchase (May 1991). It was not IMF collateral. The dates are wrong (47t was July, not May), and one counterparty is missing (Bank of Japan). The US$7bn figure is sourced by Wikipedia to a popular book (Meredith 2007). It is not an IMF figure, and it probably conflates total multilateral and bilateral support. From memory, not verified: IMF drawings were closer to about US$4bn across January–October 1991. The source is a tertiary Wikipedia sentence, and it is internally contradictory ("$7 billion from the IMF by pledging 67 tons" versus "to raise $600 million"). verdicts.baseRate:
The UPA-to-NDA slowdown is not specific to India. I computed the same World Bank series for seven peer emerging markets, 2004-14 CAGR vs 2014-24 CAGR:
- Brazil: 9.7% vs 0.8%
- Indonesia: 7.8% vs 3.7%
- Mexico: 10.0% vs 0.8%
- Turkey: 9.6% vs 2.2%
- South Africa: 13.0% vs 1.7%
- Thailand: 9.7% vs 2.7%
- Philippines: 2.6% vs 5.7%

Six of seven (about 86%) show the same sharp deceleration. That is above the 80% threshold, so the pattern does not discriminate: it reflects the global cycle (the 2004-14 emerging-market credit boom and post-2008 quantitative easing, then a strong dollar after 2014). The symmetry test also runs the opposite way to the naive spin once scaled to GDP. India's US$ GDP grew 11.1%/yr in 2004-14 and 6.3%/yr in 2014-24. External debt as a share of GDP went 17.4% (2004), then 22.4% (2014), then 19.1% (2024). Sovereign-only (PPG) CAGR was about 8.9% in 2004-14 and about 4.6% in 2014-24.
verdicts.denialFound: No denial is needed and none was found; nobody was asked. The claim is analytic and alleges no wrongdoing against any party, so no response was sought.
verdicts.innocentReading:
The boring explanation that fits the data: the gap is mainly the global cycle, shared by about 86% of peer emerging markets, together with slower US$ nominal GDP growth after 2014. Two further effects reduce the post-2014 dollar figure: the dollar strengthened, and the rupee depreciation shrank the US$ value of rupee-denominated external liabilities (FPI holdings of government securities, rupee NRI deposits). Growth and retrenchment in private corporate ECB/NRI borrowing, which is not sovereign policy, also moves the total. Scaled to GDP, the ratio rose under UPA and fell modestly under NDA. The difference is small, and the cyclical factors above can explain it.

The innocent reading as filed contains two errors:
1. "A lower 2014 base mechanically compounds faster" (in the claim text) and "compounding off a ~3.7x-larger base mechanically produces a lower percentage growth rate even under identical policy" (in innocentReading and symmetryCheck) are false. CAGR does not depend on scale. Identical policy, meaning identical growth rates, gives an identical CAGR whatever the base. A base effect only exists if absolute increments are held fixed. Even then NDA added less in absolute terms: +$259bn against +$334bn under UPA.
2. The 2013 taper tantrum points the wrong way. Rupee depreciation lowers the US$ value of rupee-denominated debt, so it depressed the UPA-window figure rather than inflating it.

The edge is also pinned to the Ministry of Finance, although about two-thirds of the stock is non-sovereign. As written, the claim does not survive. It should be kept as analytic only after the rationale is replaced with the peer base rate (about 86%) and the debt/GDP scaling.

verdicts.dateTest:
Claim as a sentence: IMF (actor) dictated India's reform programme in 1991. Two dated steps:
(1) CCFF plus first-credit-tranche drawing, January 1991, under the Chandra Shekhar government (FM Yashwant Sinha). Indian Express, 2017: "India had managed to get a bit of a breather with the first tranche of $755 million from the IMF". This came before the Rao government (sworn in June 1991), so it cannot have conditioned the Rao reforms.
(2) Stand-by arrangement (SBA): negotiated July–August 1991, Board approval October 1991. The devaluation (early July 1991) and the Industrial Policy Statement (24 July 1991) came before Board approval. That is consistent with prior actions, but equally consistent with a home-grown design. The record never states the SBA date or amount.
Gold pledge chronology is wrong in the record:
- 20 t of confiscated gold went to UBS on a sale-and-repurchase basis, 21–31 May 1991, for $200m. Chandra Shekhar government; Sinha signed the file.
- 46.91 t were pledged to the Bank of England and Bank of Japan, 4–18 July 1991, for $400m. Repurchased before December 1991.
Both were bridge borrowing from other central banks and a Swiss bank. Neither was collateral for the IMF loan.
The counter's phrase "after the 1991-93 facility was repaid" is loose. The SBA ran roughly 1991–93, but repurchases continued later in the decade (not verified this session).
verdicts.identityTest:
Actor attribution is only partly right. The structural conditions the strongestCase lists (de-licensing, trade liberalisation, opening sectors to foreign participation) are written into the World Bank Structural Adjustment Loan/Credit (report P-5678-IN, sanctioned 12 Nov 1991, $250m IBRD plus SDR 183.8m IDA). Wikipedia, Economic_liberalisation_in_India: "This specified deregulation, increased foreign direct investment, liberalisation of the trade regime...".
The IMF CCFF was compensatory financing for the oil shock with little conditionality. The SBA's core conditions were macro-stabilisation.
So "IMF" should read "IMF and World Bank (Bretton Woods conditionality)". The strongestCase's "the government pledged national gold reserves as collateral to secure the loan" names the wrong counterparty. Indian Express, 2017: "the Bank of England and the Bank of Japan were willing to lend but not without a collateral. It was pointed out to them that India was a depository of the IMF ... but that didn't help."
verdicts.baseRate:
Close to every upper-credit-tranche IMF stand-by and World Bank structural adjustment loan of 1980–95 carried policy conditionality, and many ran alongside devaluation and trade liberalisation (general knowledge, not quantified this session). "Borrowed under conditionality and then liberalised" therefore does not separate India in 1991 from other borrowers of the period. It cannot by itself show dictation as opposed to agreement.
Symmetry control:
- India's 1981 Extended Fund Facility under Indira Gandhi's Congress government carried conditionality too; India reportedly drew only part of it and ended it early (general knowledge, not verified this session).
- The 1991 reforms were continued by non-Congress governments: United Front 1996–98, NDA 1998–2004. The World Bank's own 1995 assessment, quoted by Indian Express 2010: "the reforms initiated in 1991 will not be reversed, as demonstrated by the reform plans and actions in states with non-Congress Party governments."
Applied to other governments, the same lens produces the same picture, so it is not a party-specific finding.
verdicts.denialFound:
No direct denial by the government that the IMF dictated the reforms was verified this session. WebSearch budget was exhausted and imf.org and dea.gov.in are blocked. The government's recorded response on the gold pledge: Manmohan Singh told Parliament it was a "painful necessity" (Indian Express 2017, https://indianexpress.com/article/explained/in-fact-how-govts-pledged-gold-to-pull-economy-back-from-the-brink/).
The accusing side is on record: opposition leaders called the 1991 Budget and New Industrial Policy a "command budget from the IMF" (Free Press Journal, cited in Wikipedia Economic_liberalisation_in_India).
The lenders' own record, World Bank declassified Country Economic Memoranda reported by Indian Express 2010 (https://indianexpress.com/article/news-archive/web/how-wb-imf-got-india-to-adopt-reforms-in-1991/), says they "chivvied and cajoled India into economic liberalisation". Its wording to the Rao government: "the only real options for India are whether the adjustment is made in the context of an orderly, growth-oriented adjustment program with external financial support, or through a disorderly and painful process".
That is pressure and leverage, not a written dictation.
verdicts.innocentReading: India was days from sovereign default: reserves under three weeks of imports, a downgrade below investment grade, and IMF and World Bank lending halted until a budget passed. Any government had to borrow from the Bretton Woods institutions, and their standard conditionality overlapped heavily with a liberalisation agenda already argued inside the Indian establishment since the Rajiv Gandhi-era partial reforms of the mid-1980s. The Rao–Singh team chose the sequence and in places went beyond the conditions, for example the scale of industrial de-licensing. Later governments of other parties continued the reforms after the leverage ended. Crisis plus lender leverage explains the timing and speed. Home ownership explains the content and durability. "Dictated" overstates the first and ignores the second.
verdicts.reason:
"Contested" is the right calibration and it survives. The documented record (World Bank declassified memoranda via Indian Express 2010; SAL P-5678-IN) shows strong IMF/World Bank leverage and explicit structural conditionality. It does not show that the IMF alone wrote the programme, and the reforms outlived the leverage.
The record carries a load-bearing factual error: it calls the gold pledge collateral for the IMF loan. The gold went to UBS (May 1991, $200m, Chandra Shekhar government) and to the Bank of England and Bank of Japan (July 1991, $400m) as bridge finance, not to the IMF.
The strongestCase also puts on the IMF stand-by/CCFF the structural conditions that sit in the World Bank SAL.
The only source is Wikipedia, a tertiary and internally inconsistent source: it says both "emergency loan of $7 billion from the IMF by pledging 67 tons" and that the gold went to the BoE and UBS.
The status holds, but the text must be corrected before publication.

(2) "Bhagwati–Panagariya" as pre-1991 advocates of reform has no source and is likely the wrong pairing. The pre-crisis works are Bhagwati–Desai (1970) and Bhagwati–Srinivasan (1975). The World Bank DPF page says prior actions "present the legal terms defined in the financing agreement". Essentially every IMF programme carries conditions, and 65,894 across all programmes is a global stock. The share of policy-based multilateral loans with policy conditions is about 100%, far above the 80% threshold, so "comes with policy strings" says nothing specific about India or any government. What would discriminate is the share of prior actions or triggers that require an Act of a legislature against a recorded ministry or committee position. That share has not been computed. verdicts.denialFound: No specific denial from GoI or the Bank about India was located. The search budget is exhausted, and no sansad.in Q&A was opened, so asked/not asked is unknown. What exists is the lender's general institutional position on the DPF page: "The DPF Policy emphasizes country ownership, stakeholder consultation…" and "non-earmarked general budget financing that is subject to the borrower's own implementation processes and systems" (https://www.worldbank.org/en/what-we-do/products-and-services/financing-instruments/development-policy-financing). These are lender self-descriptions, not responses to this claim.
verdicts.innocentReading: Policy-based lending pays out budget support against actions the borrowing executive agreed to, usually drawn from its own programme (Kerala PA1: "The GoK has adopted the Rebuild Kerala Development Program"). If a legislature does not act, the next tranche is not paid; the legislature is not overridden. The Kerala case shows this. Its DPO1 (P169907, 2019-06-27) set triggers for DPO2 that named legislation: "Draft River Basin Conservation and Management Authority Act has been submitted to the State Assembly" (Trigger 4) and "The GoK has amended TCP Act for risk-informed master planning" (Trigger 9). The Second Resilient Kerala DPO (P170521, US$350m) is recorded as "Dropped", and financing continued as a Program-for-Results (P174778, 2021-06-24). The reason for the drop is not documented. In 1991, the Budget and the Finance Bill went through Parliament, and the loans followed. Bypassing Parliament comes from India's own executive treaty and loan-signing design, which applies to every lender, bilateral and domestic-market alike.

The weak form ("multilateral loans carry policy conditions") is documented but applies to about 100% of such loans. The strong form ("override Parliament") has no documented instance. verdicts.identityTest: The record names the wrong authority and the wrong kind of borrowing. The Indian Kanoon order (2024-04-01, Surya Kant J.) says "the Defendant has imposed a 'Net Borrowing Ceiling' on the Plaintiff - State ... quantified as three percent of the projected Gross State Domestic Product ... INR 32,442 crores. This Net Borrowing Ceiling covered all sources of borrowings, including open market borrowings, loans from Financial Institutions, and the liabilities arising out of the Public Account". The order contains 0 hits for "Economic Affairs", "external", "externally" or "foreign". The ceiling is a Union/Ministry of Finance consent under Article 293(3) (in practice set by the Department of Expenditure), not a DEA decision on externally aided projects. Article 293(1) only covers state borrowing "within the territory of India". External loans are borrowed by the Union and passed on to the state, and DEA gates them through its screening and posing to lenders, which the order does not discuss. So "the DEA fixed Kerala's FY2023-24 ceiling" and "all state borrowing including externally aided projects needs Union consent under Article 293(3)" are identity and mechanism errors. The narrative's own counter already concedes that the "denial" Kerala documents is of borrowing room, not of external projects.

Delhi's only hit is a single pipeline operation, P517479, with an approval date of 2026-11-25. Share with none: 0 of 10. worldbank.json's per-capita lens has Kerala (LDF) at 1.9x, Tamil Nadu at 1.75x and Andhra Pradesh at 1.62x their population share under NDA. BJP-run UP is at 0.61x, MP 0.56x, Haryana 0.55x and Chhattisgarh 0.18x. The sibling adb-aiib.json records AIIB loans to Kerala, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Punjab and AP. Nothing in the record shows a gap against opposition states. On the "denied room" part, the Article 293(3) ceiling itself is 3% of GSDP for every state, so the rule does not discriminate by party.
verdicts.denialFound: No accuser is named. The record cites no opposition minister, state or party saying that DEA refused its external projects on partisan grounds. It cites only Kerala's suit, which is about the Net Borrowing Ceiling and never mentions external loans. The Union's response on that issue is in the court record (indiankanoon.org/doc/191833676/). It said Kerala "is apparently a highly debt stressed State that has mismanaged its finances" and "has the highest ratio of Pension to Total Revenue Expenditure among all States", and it pointed to "grave consequences regarding the fiscal health of the country". verdicts.innocentReading: DEA clears state external-aid proposals against a fiscal and priority screen, and the lender's own pipeline adds more filtering. That screen applies to every state: the 3%-of-GSDP ceiling, whether the state can repay, and the state's past record of using up its borrowing limit. Kerala's constraint in FY2023-24 came from its own admitted over-borrowing in FY2017-18 to FY2019-20 plus off-budget liabilities counted within the ceiling, not from its party. verdicts.dateTest: Claim as actor/act/object/time: "Chinese state lenders and SOEs (CDB, China Eximbank, ICBC, BOC) took control of Indian infrastructure companies before 2020." Lending window per the AidData rows in bilateral-china.json runs 2008-06 (CDB Facility I to RCom) to 2015-03 (CDB to Aircel). The only coercive acts fall inside the window: CDB's NCLT insolvency petition against RCom (2017-11), withdrawn 2018-01-05, and RCom's insolvency (2019-02). None of these is a transfer of control. The Ambani judgment (UK High Court, 2020-05-22) falls after the "before 2020" cutoff and enforces a personal guarantee. It is not an equity or board step-in. Press Note 3 (2020-04-18) also comes after the window and governs equity, not these loans. On Brookings: the "five-fold to at least US$8 billion" covers the three years after 2014, so roughly 2017. That matches the narrative's "by 2017".

The Chinese lenders are named state policy banks and commercial banks, not a nationality acting as one bloc. The claim's actor, "Chinese money", is a nationality-level abstraction. Under CONTRACT rule 1 that belongs only in narratives, never as an edge. Brookings (Ananth Krishnan, 2020-03-30) refers to "official figures", meaning MOFCOM FDI data, not "official finance" in the AidData sense. The narrative's phrase "official Chinese FDI" mixes the two. Banking on Beijing (Dreher, Fuchs, Parks, Strange, Tierney 2022) mentions "corruption, political capture, and conflict" as general risks for low- and middle-income countries. India is not named on the opened page.

SEK and the Nordic Investment Bank co-financed Aircel. In the RCom insolvency, CDB held about 37% of RCom's secured debt (c039), a large but not controlling creditor position. The bilateral-china.json analytic (c061) finds that 3 of the 4 largest Chinese-bank borrowers went insolvent (RCom, Aircel, Lanco). That default rate matches the wider 2015–19 stress in Indian telecom and thermal power, where Indian public-sector banks carried most of the losses. Default is not a distinguishing feature of Chinese-financed borrowers. On sovereign books China records zero PPG debt, against Japan's 72% of India's PPG bilateral debt (c060). The same capture lens applied to the Japanese control gives a more concentrated picture (tied MAHSR procurement, a 50-year creditor to a Union PSU). The alarm is therefore a property of the lens, as the file's symmetryCheck already says.
verdicts.denialFound: Ambani's spokesperson (The Wire, 2020-05-22, recorded as contra bilateral-china:c042) said the guarantee was "never signed by Ambani" and that the debt was "not a personal loan" but RCom's 2012 corporate refinancing: https://thewire.in/business/uk-court-orders-anil-ambani-to-pay-717-million-to-chinese-banks-within-21-days. No response from CDB, China Eximbank or ICBC was found, and none was asked for. No Indian government statement claiming Chinese control of an infrastructure company before 2020 was found. PN3's stated purpose is "curbing opportunistic takeovers/acquisitions" during COVID-19, which is forward-looking.
verdicts.innocentReading: Between 2008 and 2015, Indian private telecom and power companies borrowed dollar credit from Chinese policy banks. Much of it was buyer's credit tied to Chinese equipment (Shanghai Electric turbines and boilers, Chinese telecom gear) and priced at LIBOR plus 1.8–4.75%. It was ordinary commercial export credit, the same instrument US Ex-Im and the Nordic ECAs gave the same sectors. When the borrowers failed in the 2017–19 telecom and power bust, the Chinese banks acted like any secured creditor: an NCLT petition, which was withdrawn, then a vote in the IBC committee of creditors alongside Indian banks, then a UK guarantee claim. The Chinese equity that did arrive went mostly into technology and pharma stakes and start-ups. The infrastructure figures were pledges and bids "as yet unapproved" (about US$15bn, per Brookings).
verdicts.reason: The claim is refuted as an assertion, and the file's "unsupported" calibration survives. None of the three sources shows a Chinese entity with control, a board seat or step-in rights over an Indian infrastructure company before 2020. Brookings says the opposite for the relevant period: the investment was "predominantly state-owned enterprises (SOEs)" only in the pre-2014 US$1.6bn stock. After that it records "a noticeable shift from state-driven to market-driven investment from the Chinese private sector". It places "controlling stakes" in "the technology sector", and describes the infrastructure money as pledges "in bids for major infrastructure projects that are as yet unapproved". The AidData rows in bilateral-china.json are all debt (c052). The strongestCase is a conjunction of true facts (large Chinese credit, borrower defaults, a 2020 guarantee judgment, PN3) that together suggest "capture" when no single source says it. The status should not move to "debunked" yet. Chinese lenders sat on IBC committees of creditors for RCom, Aircel and Lanco in 2018–19, and those committees legally control a corporate debtor's resolution. The Chinese voting shares have not been verified, and DPIIT equity data was not opened. The narrative should stay a narrative (nationality as actor) at status "unsupported", with the fixes below.

Only the change between periods is distinctive, and the file's symmetry check finds the lens gives dispersed, 'alarming-looking' ratios in both periods and for both blocs. In 2000-02 it received about US$824m (GSHP-I US$381m, Earthquake Reconstruction US$443m), under NDA-I, and this came from need (the 2001 earthquake) and the project cycle. verdicts.innocentReading: The record's own innocent reading applies. States borrow through DEA under Article 293. The state pipeline and FRBM borrowing headroom determine uptake. In the UPA years Gujarat's pipeline existed but was dropped (Urban Services US$350m in 2005, Urban Reform US$100m in 2007). Adding the separate GOAL-AF US$250m on top counts US$250m twice or wrongly, which inflates Gujarat's NDA total from US$1,380m to US$1,630m. The same curr_total_commitment problem inflates the state-attributed denominator: projects where total exceeds IBRD+IDA include Amaravati 1600/800, Kerala 370/125, Chennai 300/150, Punjab 210/105 and WB irrigation 290/145. The direction (a low UPA-era share rising to above population share under NDA) survives, and the analytic tier with an innocentReading is the right tier once the numbers are fixed. The UPA figures (US$175m, 1.5%, 0.29x) check out against the API.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim: IBRD/IDA commitments to AP rose from 0.35x population share under UPA (2004-05-22 to 2014-05-25) to 1.62x under NDA (2014-05-26 to 2026-09-26). Approval dates are in the right windows. P507508 Amaravati Integrated Urban Development Program: boardapprovaldate 2024-12-19, which is correct and falls under the TDP-led NDA-ally government (June 2024 on). The statement that the rise spans TDP, YSRCP and TDP-NDA governments misstates the politics. TDP was an NDA ally from 2014 to March 2018, and P155038 AP 24x7 Power (US$400m, 2017-05-26) was approved while it was an ally. The earlier Amaravati project, P159808 (US$300m IBRD), was Dropped in 2019 under YSRCP. So the largest single item exists only because of the 2024 NDA-ally government. It is not evidence of continuity across opposition governments.
verdicts.identityTest: Failed on the node's scope. The population denominator is undivided AP (Census 2011, 7.2%), and the NDA numerator includes a Telangana project (P143608, US$75m). The UPA numerator, however, leaves out every undivided-AP project that the API now labels 'Andhra Pradesh and Telangana' or that names both states' agencies. Those are P100789 (US$189m, 2007), P101650 (US$150m, 2009), P096021 (US$320m, 2009), P071250 (US$300m, 2009) and P100954 (US$450.6m, 2010), about US$1,410m in total. They were single-state loans to undivided AP, relabelled after the 2014 bifurcation, and the regex put them in the 'US$1.4bn multi-state' bucket. The UPA figure of US$292m is exactly P075174 (225) + P104724 (65) + P122241 (1.9) = 291.9. Also, Amaravati's curr_total_commitment of US$1,600m includes co-financing. The API's own curr_ibrd_commitment for P507508 is 800,000,000, so the Bank's own loan is US$800m, not US$1,600m.
verdicts.baseRate: The record's own symmetryCheck says the per-capita lens is 'alarming' in both periods and for both blocs: 11 of 25 states are above 1.5x under NDA, and dispersion is similar under UPA. Once the UPA undivided-AP loans are restored, AP comes to about US$1,701m out of about US$13,209m state-attributed, a 12.9% share against 7.2% of population, or about 1.79x under UPA. That is above the NDA figure of 1.62x. If only the Bank's own IBRD share of Amaravati (US$800m) is counted, the NDA ratio falls further, to roughly 1.1-1.2x. The 'rise' becomes a flat or falling ratio. AP was above parity under both UPA and NDA, so the property does not discriminate.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable: this is an analytic comparison and no wrongdoing is alleged. None found; the parties were not asked (DEA, the AP Finance Department and the World Bank India office).
verdicts.innocentReading: Undivided AP was one of the Bank's main state partners under UPA: the 2004-10 economic reform loans, roads, municipal, water sector, tanks and RWSS projects. After 2014 the API relabelled those projects as AP-and-Telangana, and the attribution regex reclassified them as multi-state. That created an artificially low UPA baseline. The post-2014 figure is dominated by one 2024 co-financed Amaravati programme (US$800m WB + ADB) that restarts a 2016-19 pipeline. That is timing, not a change of regime.
verdicts.reason: This is a methodological artefact. The UPA baseline of 0.35x (US$292m) leaves out about US$1.41bn of World Bank loans to undivided Andhra Pradesh in 2007-2010 (P100789, P101650, P096021, P071250, P100954). The same API relabels them 'Andhra Pradesh and Telangana', and the regex binned them as multi-state. Yet the NDA numerator includes Telangana and the population denominator is undivided AP. Corrected, UPA is about 1.79x, which is at or above the NDA 1.62x, so the headline 'rise' disappears. Separately, the US$1,600m Amaravati figure is the programme total. The API gives curr_ibrd_commitment as US$800m for P507508.

verdicts.dateTest: Restated: "IBRD/IDA board approvals for India attributable to one state were 31% of commitments under UPA (2004-05-22 to 2014-05-25) and 52% under NDA (2014-05-26 to 2026-09-26)." Most of the states above 1.5x (8 of 11, not 7: Tripura is north-eastern and was miscounted) have under 1% of India's population each, so one project of US$100-300m pushes the ratio past 1.5x. Under UPA the same lens gives HP about 7x, Uttarakhand about 4x and Puducherry above 13x, so the shape is the same in both eras. The rise in state share is method-sensitive: recomputing from research/raw/finance/worldbank-projects.json (IBRD+IDA only, Dropped and pipeline projects excluded, pre-fetched state field) gives about 38% under UPA (US$13.6bn of US$36.0bn) and about 53% under NDA (US$23.6bn of US$44.9bn). The direction holds, but the UPA figure moves by 7 points depending on the attribution rule. Haryana comes out at 0.61x with P510686 (US$300m, 2025-12-10) included, which is borderline for "below 0.6x".
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable. This is our own analytic comparison and accuses no party of anything, so no denial was sought or found (none found, not asked).
verdicts.innocentReading: Small states get high per-capita ratios mechanically. Projects take 2-4 years to prepare, so the pipeline lags any change of government. The Bank moved toward state-level operations and PforRs after 2014, and IDA graduation removed cheap central credits. State FRBM ceilings and implementing capacity limit borrowing. State external borrowing is routed through DEA under Article 293. Any of these explains both the rising state share and the scatter of ratios without reference to party. The stored innocentReading already says this and is adequate.
verdicts.reason: The headline shares (31% to 52%) survive only as a method-dependent analytic figure. The party half of the claim fails the date test. It says "no party pattern" and supports that with labels that are wrong at the approval dates. Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu are called "southern opposition-run", but most of AP's money (including the US$800m Amaravati programme) and most of TN's pre-2021 money was approved under NDA-allied governments. Chhattisgarh is called "BJP-run" below 0.6x, but every one of its NDA-era projects was approved under Congress. Most of the hill and north-eastern states above 1.5x were BJP- or NDA-governed when their loans were approved. The claim also miscounts the hill/north-eastern group as 7 of 11 when it is 8. If the ratios are joined to ruling party by approval date, they do not show the neutral mix the text describes. They lean NDA-aligned, and small-state denominators and pipeline timing explain that lean. So the defensible statement is "party cannot be separated from state size and timing on this lens", not "no party pattern". The claim as worded does not survive, and it needs correcting before it can stay analytic.

verdicts.dateTest: Stated as a claim: the World Bank (IBRD and IDA) financed measures the Government of India (MoF/DEA) had already announced, 2020–23. The 2020 dates hold. PMGKY was announced 26 March 2020; the P173943 Program Document says "measures announced on March 25, 2020", a one-day difference. P173943 was approved 2020-05-14, and the PD itself is dated April 30, 2020. ECLGS was announced 13–17 May 2020 (PD: "The Program announced during May 13 - 17, 2020"), and the WB API shows P174292 approved 2020-06-30. MSME PA#5 is the RBI sandbox, "circular issued on August 13, 2019". PA#7 is PSB59, which the PD says was "Launched in November 2018". So for all three 2020 COVID operations the measures came before approval. The 2023 end of the window fails. The P181032 CCTS notification (Trigger #6) was issued 2023-06-28, one day before board approval, and was designed with Bank technical assistance (TA), so "already announced, not shaped by the Bank" does not hold for 2023.

verdicts.baseRate: Close to 100%. Under World Bank DPF policy, prior actions are by definition measures the borrower completes before Board presentation. Every DPF for every borrower, including UPA-era Indian DPLs such as the 2009 US$2bn Banking Sector Support DPL, has prior actions that predate approval. Showing that the prior actions predate approval therefore says nothing about who authored the policy. It is a definitional truism. The SPEC's UPA-vs-NDA control was not run.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable. No party is accused. No World Bank or MoF statement on authorship was found, and none was asked for.
verdicts.innocentReading: The Bank's DPF instrument rewards completed government actions. In an emergency (2020) the Bank picked prior actions from GoI's announced COVID package. In programmatic series (2023) it co-designs reforms through analytical work and TA, then counts them as prior actions. Neither pattern shows capture in either direction.
verdicts.reason: The record's own killIf condition is met by a source the record itself cites. The P181032 Program Document (Low-Carbon DPL, 2023) says Bank TA "provided inputs to the National Green Hydrogen Roadmap, the NGHM", and lists underpinnings for PA #9 ("Supported BEE in designing the carbon market in India", through the partnership-for-market-readiness TA), PA #10 ("Supported SEBI to amend the existing regulations") and PA #11 ("Supported the MoF on the design of the Sovereign Green Bond Framework"). The MSME PD lists "IFC TA on Regulatory Sandbox" as the underpinning for PA#5. So "the Bank financed the package rather than dictating it" is refuted for 2023 and weakened for one 2020 action. "Dictating" is also a strawman: the documented middle case is Bank TA shaping measures that GoI then adopts. The claim's examples of the "real conditionality" (the SEBI ESG and carbon-market triggers) were themselves Bank-supported designs. The amount does not reconcile either. The file's own loan edges give 1,508 + 4,147 (P173943) + 2,960 (P174027) + 5,673 (P174292) = ₹14,288 cr, not ₹14,328 cr. Adding P181032 (₹12,431 cr) would give ₹26,719 cr, yet the text says "2020–23". Benefit confidence is marked "documented" for a total that no source states and that does not add up. What survives is a narrow analytic note: the three 2020 COVID operations financed measures already announced.
